Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the primary and secondary restraints involved in medial elbow stability.
Discuss the pertinent anatomy of the proximal and distal ulnar collateral ligament and the
forearm flexor pronator group and their relationship to surrounding neurovascular structures.
Explain the mechanisms of ulnar collateral injury in throwing athletes.
Review the indications, risks, advantages, and outcomes of nonsurgical management of ulnar
collateral ligament injuries.
Review the indications, risks, advantages, and outcomes of surgical management of ulnar
collateral ligament injuries.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

The medial ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) complex consists of the anterior oblique ligament,
the posterior oblique ligament, and the transverse ligament.
The anterior oblique ligament is the strongest and is the primary stabilizer to valgus stress. It
is composed of anterior and posterior bands that provide reciprocal function in resisting
valgus stress through range of flexion-extension motion.
The anterior band is taut in extension, and the posterior band is tight in flexion.
The UCL originates from the anteroinferior surface of the medial epicondyle, just posterior to
the elbow center of rotation, and inserts at the sublime tubercle of the ulna (Figure 1).
Injuries to the UCL can result from acute trauma during elbow dislocations; however, most
isolated injuries result from repetitive valgus forces applied to the medial elbow in throwing
athletes, specifically during the late cocking/early acceleration phase of throwing.
Figure 1 Anterior (A) and medial (B) view illustrations of an elbow show the three bundles of the
ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) and the relationship between the anterior bundle of the UCL and
the musculotendinous insertions of the flexor pronator mass, with the footprints represented by
different colors. ABUCL = anterior bundle of the UCL, FCU = ulnar carpi ulnaris, FDS = flexor

digitorum superficialis, OBUCL = oblique bundle of the UCL, PBUCL = posterior bundle of the UCL,
PT = pronator teres. (Reproduced with permission from Frangiamore SJ, Moatshe G, Kruckeberg
BM, et al: Qualitative and quantitative analyses of the dynamic and static stabilizers of the medial
elbow: An anatomic study. Am J Sports Med 2018;46[3]:687-694.)
Epidemiology
Injuries to the UCL traditionally occur in overhead athletes who subject the elbow to
tremendous valgus forces.
Of all overhead athletes, baseball players and javelin throwers most commonly sustain UCL
injuries.
Tears can occur in the midsubstance of the ligament or as avulsions from the proximal origin
or distal insertion.
Elbow dislocation or a fall onto an outstretched hand also can result in an UCL injury.

Epidemiology
UCL injuries are observed in throwing athletes because of the repetitive valgus stress
placed on the elbow during overhead throwing. Valgus torque generated at the elbow
during throwing maneuvers is highest in the late cocking and early acceleration phases
and may result in attenuation, insufficiency, or rupture of the UCL, which typically
manifest as medial elbow pain and decreased throwing performance, evidenced by
reduced velocity, poor control, and decreased endurance.1-3 Athletes who play baseball
for more than 8 months per year, pitch more than 100 innings per year, and have high
pitch counts during competition have an increased risk for UCL injuries. Throwers with
fatigue also are at risk for an UCL injury, regardless of age.4 As many as one-third of
professional baseball pitchers have undergone surgical treatment for an UCL injury, and
the prevalence is increasing, especially in the minor leagues.4,5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
3/23

The osseous stabilizers of the elbow include the radiocapitellar and ulnohumeral articulations.
These bony articulations provide stability at angles of elbow flexion of less than 20° and more
than 120° and provide as much as 2° of rotary stability.6
The center of the UCL origin is approximately 8 mm anterior and 8 mm distal to the center of
the medial aspect of the medial epicondyle and has a broad insertion that extends from the
sublime tubercle distally along the ulnar ridge.
The olecranon stabilizes valgus stress to the elbow, and excessive resection of the olecranon
places the UCL at risk.
Joints and Ligaments
The UCL complex consists of three ligaments: the anterior oblique, posterior oblique, and
transverse ligaments (Figure 2).
The anterior oblique ligament is the strongest and is the primary stabilizer to valgus stress. It
is composed of anterior and posterior bands that provide reciprocal function in resisting
valgus stress through the range of flexion-extension motion.
The anterior band is taut in extension, and the posterior band is tight in flexion.
The anterior oblique ligament originates on the anteroinferior edge of the medial epicondyle
and inserts on the sublime tubercle of the ulna.
The anterior bundle of the UCL is one of the primary static constraints of the elbow, along
with the ulnohumeral articulation and the lateral UCL complex.
Figure 2 Illustrations of an elbow show the structure of the medial collateral ligament complex
(A) and the lateral collateral ligament complex (B). (Reproduced with permission from Tashjian
RZ, Katarincic JA: Complex elbow instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[5]:278-286.)
SEND FEEDBACK

Muscles
The dynamic stabilizers of the elbow are made up of the flexor pronator muscle complex that
crosses the elbow joint: the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU),
pronator teres, and brachialis7 (Figure 3)
Within the flexor pronator mass, the FDS and FCU provide a dynamic stabilizing force across
the elbow joint and may be protective of the static restraint of the UCL.7
The FDS and FCU ulnar attachments overlap the UCL, creating an intimate relationship
between the UCL and the flexor pronator mass. The FCU ulnar limb overlaps the UCL footprint,
and the FDS has a tendinous ulnar attachment just medial to the ulnar ridge, with fibers
attached to the anterior bundle of the UCL.7,8
Figure 3 Medial view illustration of an elbow shows the three bundles of the ulnar collateral
ligament (UCL) and the relationship between the anterior bundle of the UCL and the
musculotendinous insertions of the flexor pronator mass. ABUCL = anterior bundle of the UCL,
FCU = ulnar carpi ulnaris, FDS = flexor digitorum superficialis, OBUCL = oblique bundle of the

UCL, PBUCL = posterior bundle of the UCL. (Reproduced with permission from Frangiamore SJ,
Moatshe G, Kruckeberg BM, et al: Qualitative and quantitative analyses of the dynamic and static
stabilizers of the medial elbow: An anatomic study. Am J Sports Med 2018;46[3]:687-694.)

Muscles
The anterior bundle of the UCL has a humeral footprint 15.4 mm from the joint line and
an ulnar footprint 5.8 to 7.8 mm from the joint line. The center of the ulnar footprint is
1.5 to 7.6 mm distal to the center of the sublime tubercle. The overall length of the
bundle (including footprint) is 51 to 53 mm. Historically, the ulnar footprint of the UCL
was thought to insert directly on the sublime tubercle without distal extent; however,
more recent studies have shown that it is elongated and tapered.8,9 The ulnar footprint
is important because it leads to an intimate relationship between the UCL and the
dynamic stabilizers of the elbow, the flexor pronator muscles. Forty-six percent of the
length of the FDS ulnar tendinous insertion overlaps the anterior bundle of the UCL.10
Similarly, during the proximal to distal course of the FCU ulnar insertion, 21% overlaps
with the anterior bundle of the UCL.10 Numerous biomechanical studies have confirmed
the importance of the flexor pronator muscle group in providing dynamic stability to
valgus stress.7-9 Throwers with an UCL injury have a high incidence of concomitant flexor
pronator mass injuries, and electromyography shows evidence of decreased activity with
valgus instability.10
Mechanism and Pattern of Injury
Elbow dislocation
The lateral collateral ligament complex is disrupted in all elbow dislocations. Some surgeons
believe that the UCL is always disrupted with elbow dislocation; however, this is
controversial.
Injury to the UCL in throwers
UCL injuries occur in overhead athletes because of the repetitive valgus forces of throwing.
Pitching velocity and volume are risk factors for injury.
Valgus torque generated at the elbow during throwing is highest in the late cocking and early
acceleration phases of throwing.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
6/23

Acute valgus instability in nonthrowers
Valgus instability also can result from a fall onto an outstretched hand and a direct valgus
load.
Injury to the anterior band of the UCL is the essential lesion.

Mechanism and Pattern of Injury
Although UCL injuries can result from elbow dislocations and falls in nonthrowers, the
most common mechanism of injury is repetitive overhead throwing. The prevalence of
UCL injuries continues to rise at the professional and amateur levels.4 In professional
baseball, more than 10% of all players and 25% of pitchers have a history of UCL
reconstruction.6 Throwing-related injuries are the result of repetitive valgus stress at the
elbow, which can exceed five times an athlete’s body weight.11 As the arm transitions
from cocking to acceleration, the elbow lags behind the trunk.2 This transition can
increase overall elbow torque and place considerable stress on the UCL. Pitching velocity
and volume are documented risk factors for UCL injury in throwing athletes.4
Associated Injuries
Ulnar neuritis
The ulnar nerve is closely related to the UCL because the UCL forms the floor of the cubital
tunnel.12
Repetitive tensile force on the ulnar nerve may cause ulnar neuritis. The throwing motion
subjects the elbow to considerable valgus stress, placing traction on the ulnar nerve. The
early acceleration phase causes a mean ulnar nerve strain of 5% to 13%.12
Ulnar neuritis may result from UCL injury because increased elbow valgus laxity from UCL
insufficiency may cause elongation of the ulnar nerve and exacerbate cubital tunnel
syndrome during the throwing motion.12
Flexor pronator strain
Flexor pronator injuries often accompany UCL injuries because static stability is
compromised, increasing stress on dynamic stabilizers.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
7/23

Patients often have pain over the medial epicondyle more proximal and anterior than the
typical UCL injury.
Valgus extension overload syndrome
During throwing, the olecranon is repeatedly and forcefully driven into the olecranon fossa,
exerting shear forces on the medial aspect of the olecranon tip and the olecranon fossa,
which may cause cartilage injury and the development of osteophytes.
Concomitant medial ligamentous laxity from an UCL strain, partial tear, or complete tear may
exacerbate the condition.
Injury Classification (MRI-Based Classification)
13
Grade 1A: partial tear of the proximal/humeral UCL
Grade 1B: complete tear of the proximal/humeral UCL
Grade 2A: partial tear of the midsubstance UCL
Grade 2B: complete tear of the midsubstance UCL
Grade 3A: partial tear of the distal/ulnar UCL
Grade 3B: complete tear of the distal/ulnar UCL
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients with UCL injuries report medial elbow pain during the acceleration phase of throwing;
pain may occur only if throwing at more than 50% to 75% of maximal effort.5
Acute injuries may present suddenly, with a pop, sharp pain, and inability to continue
throwing.
Physical Examination
Point tenderness may be noted at the UCL or toward its insertion sites.
Static valgus instability is tested via applied valgus stress while flexing the elbow between 20°
and 30° to unlock the olecranon from its fossa.
The milking maneuver is performed by having the patient or the examiner pull on the
patient’s thumb to create valgus stress as the patient’s forearm is supinated and the elbow is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
8/23

flexed beyond 90°. A subjective feeling of apprehension, instability, or localized pain at the
UCL indicates injury.5
The moving valgus stress test is a modification of the milking maneuver. Valgus stress is
applied as the elbow is moved through an arc of flexion or extension.5 A subjective feeling of
apprehension, instability, or localized pain at the UCL indicates injury.5 This is considered the
most sensitive and specific test for diagnosis14 (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Clinical photograph shows the moving valgus stress test, which is performed with the
patient in the supine position. (Reproduced with permission from Tashjian RZ, Wolf BR, van Riet
RP, Steinmann SP: The unstable elbow: Current concepts in diagnosis and treatment. Instr Course
Lect 2016;65:55-82.)
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Lateral, AP, and axillary views should be obtained to assess for joint space narrowing,
osteophytes, and loose bodies.
Valgus stress radiographs with the elbow in 20° to 30° of flexion and the forearm in full
supination may be obtained to measure the medial joint line opening; more than 3 mm is

considered diagnostic for valgus instability.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (Figure 5)
Conventional MRI may help identify thickening within the ligament from chronic injury or more
obvious full-thickness tears.
Magnetic resonance arthrography enhanced with intra-articular gadolinium contrast improves
the diagnosis of partial undersurface tears.
Figure 5 Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of an elbow shows a complete medial collateral ligament tear
(circle). (Reproduced with permission from Tashjian RZ, Wolf BR, van Riet RP, Steinmann SP: The
unstable elbow: Current concepts in diagnosis and treatment. Instr Course Lect 2016;65:55-82.)
Ultrasonography
Dynamic ultrasonography may help detect increased laxity with valgus stress; however, the
diagnostic quality of the results is operator dependent.
Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
10/23

Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonathletes can be treated nonsurgically, with good results.
Throwing athletes with a partial tear may respond well to nonsurgical management.
Contraindications
Throwing athletes with a complete tear, especially pitchers, usually are treated surgically.
Depending on the tissue quality and level of play, repair versus reconstruction can be
considered.
Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management includes a period of rest followed by a structured interval throwing
program. Physical therapy involves evaluation and optimization of the entire kinetic chain.
Flexor pronator strengthening and optimization of throwing mechanics are followed by a
progressive throwing program or reduced throwing demands.
Failure is defined as recurrence of pain after the initiation or progression of throwing.
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) or other biologic injections can augment physical therapy regimens.
Outcomes
Nonthrowing athletes typically have good outcomes with nonsurgical treatment. Throwing
athletes, specifically pitchers, have less favorable outcomes with nonsurgical treatment.
In throwing athletes, tear location (proximal versus distal) may influence the success of
nonsurgical treatment.
Biologics, such as PRP injections, have shown mixed but overall favorable results as an adjunct
to nonsurgical treatment in throwers.15

Nonsurgical Management
Studies on nonsurgical treatment in throwing athletes have demonstrated mixed results,
and failed nonsurgical treatment may result in two lost seasons if surgical treatment
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
11/23

ultimately is warranted.10,16-18 MRI studies have shown that patients with a complete
tear have poorer outcomes with nonsurgical treatment compared with patients with a
partial tear. Ulnar-sided distal tears fail at higher rates compared with proximal tears in
professional pitchers.10,19 The poorest outcomes of distal tears may be related to
decreased blood supply, the proximity of the flexor attachments to the ulnar footprint,
or other biomechanical factors.10,20 Biologics, including PRP, may be used to facilitate
healing and return to play but are associated with mixed results in augmenting a rest-
and-return-to-throwing program.21,22 Podesta et al23 described a rehabilitation and
return-to-throwing algorithm that included only gentle range of motion for the first 2
weeks after PRP injections under ultrasonographic guidance. Strengthening of the upper
extremity is initiated approximately 3 weeks after PRP injection, and some valgus
stretching is added to the program 5 to 6 weeks after the injection. Strengthening is then
increased gradually, and a throwing program is initiated 8 to 10 weeks after injection if
the patient is symptom free. Return to play is allowed 12 to 14 weeks after the PRP
injection. In this study, the authors reported that 88% of athletes (30 of 34) who used
this algorithm successfully returned to high-level play. Similarly, Deal et al21 instituted a
physical therapy program augmented with PRP injections in 23 throwing athletes, 22 of
whom (96%) were able to return to play and demonstrated reconstitution of the medial
UCL on MRI. Using the major league baseball injury tracking database, Chauhan et al16
compared professional baseball players with an UCL injury managed nonsurgically with
and without PRP and reported no notable difference in the success of nonsurgical
treatment or time to return to play. Despite some evidence supporting the use of PRP
therapy in patients with a partial UCL tear, no current consensus exists regarding the
true efficacy of PRP therapy, and research into its application is ongoing.24
Surgical Management
Indications
Acute, complete ligament tears or avulsions in competitive throwing athletes, specifically
pitchers
Partial symptomatic tears in high-level pitchers, especially those in whom nonsurgical
treatment has failed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
12/23

In nonpitchers, nonsurgical treatment usually is attempted extensively before considering
reconstruction or repair.
Although UCL repair is controversial, it may be considered in amateur overhead athletes if
MRIs show an avulsion of the ligament from the sublime tubercle or the medial epicondyle
with good to normal ligament tissue quality.
Contraindications
Asymptomatic athletes with low valgus demands on the elbow and patients who cannot or are
unwilling to undergo an extensive postoperative rehabilitation program
Techniques and Procedures
Preoperative Planning
The decision to perform elbow arthroscopy before UCL reconstruction should be made
preoperatively based on physical examination findings and imaging studies.
If spurring is observed posteromedially on imaging studies and the clinical examination is
consistent with posteromedial impingement, then elbow arthroscopy is performed to
débride the superior medial olecranon and the medial olecranon.
If patients have concomitant articular cartilage injury, loose bodies, and synovitis, these
pathologies can be managed via elbow arthroscopy before UCL reconstruction.
Patient Positioning
The patient should be placed in the supine or prone position for UCL reconstruction.
Occasionally, prone positioning is preferred because it places the elbow in a varus position
and optimizes visualization for the surgeon and the assistant during the procedure (Figure
6).
Prone positioning also allows for easy elbow arthroscopy, which often is performed before
UCL reconstruction.

Steinmann SP: The unstable elbow: Current concepts in diagnosis and treatment. Instr Course Lect

Surgical Approaches
Various techniques have been described for reconstruction, including the modified Jobe
technique (Figure 7, A), the docking technique (Figure 7, B), and the hybrid interference screw
technique (Figure 7, C).
Techniques vary with regard to the manner in which the graft configured and fixed and with
regard to the management of soft tissue and the ulnar nerve.
Reconstruction typically is performed with the use of autograft, specifically ipsilateral or
contralateral palmaris longus or gracilis tendon harvested from the contralateral knee.
UCL repair with or without internal brace augmentation is associated with encouraging results,
with less invasive surgical management and faster rehabilitation; however, current research is
limited, and additional studies with longer-term follow-up are neessary.25,26

Figure 7 Drawings show the surgical techniques for medial collateral ligament reconstruction. A,
Modified Jobe technique with muscle-splitting approach, figure-of-8 reconstruction, and ulnar
nerve in situ. B, Docking technique with graft limbs tensioned into the humeral docking tunnel. C,
Hybrid reconstruction technique with interference screw fixation on the ulna and docking fixation
on the humerus. (Panel A adapted with permission from Kvitne RS, Jobe FW: Ligamentous and
posterior compartment injuries, in Jobe FW, ed: Operative Techniques in Upper Extremity Sports
Injuries. St. Louis, MO, Mosby, 1996, pp 411-430. Panels B and C reproduced from Ahmad CS,
ElAttrache NS: Elbow valgus instability in the throwing athlete. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2006;14[12]:693-700.)

Surgical Approaches
Dr. Frank Jobe first performed UCL reconstruction on pitcher Tommy John in 1974, which
involved detaching the flexor pronator mass from the medial epicondyle for visualization
of the UCL, leaving a carpet of tissue for subsequent repair.27 Since his original
description, many variations of reconstruction have been described and multiple
modifications have been reported, including the modified Jobe technique via a flexor-
pronator muscle-splitting approach; the American Sports Medicine Institute technique;
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
15/23

the docking procedure; the modified docking procedure (Video 1); and the David
Altchek, Neal ElAttrache, Tommy John technique.28 The main differences between the
techniques involve graft fixation methods, management of the ulnar nerve, and graft
configuration. Although no studies have shown a clear benefit of one technique over
another, studies directly comparing various surgical techniques are lacking.29 The
docking technique, which has increased in popularity, was developed to reduce
disruption of the common flexor origin via a muscle-splitting rather than a muscle-
elevating approach and to reduce the risk of injury to the ulnar nerve by avoiding routine
transposition.30
Video 1 Chalmers PN, Cohen MS, Erickson B, Romeo AA: Double Docking Technique for
Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/18337__Videos. Accessed June 2, 2021.
Postoperative Management
In the immediate postoperative period, the patient’s elbow is placed in a splint for 7 to 10 days
and then transitioned to a hinged elbow brace, which allows for motion from 45° to 90°.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
16/23

Full motion is gradually restored during a 6-week period.
Throwing usually is initiated after specific strength parameters are achieved, at approximately
4 to 6 months postoperatively.
After a successful return-to-throwing program, return to play after reconstruction occurs at
approximately 12 to 18 months postoperatively.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve commonly is encountered during the surgical
approach, most often over the flexor pronator musculature. The nerve should be carefully
mobilized and retracted to avoid injury during reconstruction or repair.
Anatomic tunnel positioning is key to achieve graft isometry during reconstruction.
Care should be taken to minimize retraction on the ulnar nerve during UCL reconstruction.
Valgus stress is avoided until 4 months postoperatively.
Complications
Complications include ulnar nerve or medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve injury, ulnar or
epicondylar fracture, elbow stiffness, and failure to achieve preinjury level of throwing ability.
Rehabilitation
Active wrist, elbow, and shoulder range-of-motion exercises are initiated early in the
postoperative period.
Strengthening exercises begin at 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively; however, valgus stress is
avoided until 4 months postoperatively.
A progressive throwing program is initiated at 4 months postoperatively.
A return to competitive throwing is permitted at 1 year postoperatively if the shoulder, elbow,
and forearm are pain free and full range of motion has returned.
Outcomes
In general, surgical outcomes after UCL reconstruction are good, with an overall return-to-
sport rate of 80% to 90% and a mean return-to-play time of 12 to 18 months postoperatively.
Overall, a 10.4% complication rate (transient ulnar neuritis is the most frequent complication)
has been reported, which is more common with the Jobe technique versus the docking
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
17/23

technique.31
Concomitant flexor pronator mass tear, ulnohumeral chondromalacia, and native UCL
ligament calcification are associated with inferior outcomes and lower return-to-sport rates
after UCL reconstruction.
Repair of the UCL via internal brace augmentation recently has been shown to result in
promising early outcomes (92% return to play at a mean of 6.7 months) in carefully selected
throwers.32
Pearls and Pitfalls
Proper tunnel placement on the humeral and ulnar sides is essential for graft isometry.
Ulnar nerve complications can occur.
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, which lies at the distal aspect of the incision, can be
injured during dissection.

Pearls and Pitfalls
The original Jobe technique resulted in a return-to-play rate of 62.5% to 68%, which is
considerably lower than more modern techniques because of soft-tissue and ulnar nerve
problems related to detachment of the flexor pronator muscle group.28 In a systematic
review, Erickson et al31 reported an overall return-to-sport rate of 86.2%, with a higher
return in collegiate athletes (95.5%) compared with high school (89.4%) or professional
athletes (86.4%).
Biomechanical studies have demonstrated favorable results with docking technique
compared with other techniques;33,34 however, multiple studies of throwing athletes at
different levels have shown no notable differences with regard to return to play or
return to the same level of play in comparing graft configuration (eg, docking; modified
Jobe; American Sports Medicine Institute; and the David Altchek, Neal ElAttrache, and
Tommy John techniques), fixation, and graft selection (palmaris versus gracilis).3,29,35
Traditionally, early studies on UCL repair yielded poor results, with return-to-play rates
lower than 71.4% and as low as 29% in Major League Baseball athletes.36,37
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:40 PM
AAOS | Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004074
18/23

Dugas et al8 described the augmentation of UCL repair with the use of a collagen-coated
suture that biomechanically demonstrated less medial joint gapping and similar
resistance to failure. The authors reported a 92% return to the same or higher level of
competition at a mean time of 6.7 months, demonstrating return-to-play rates similar to
those of traditional UCL reconstruction despite a considerably shorter rehabilitation
time. Although these initial results are encouraging in younger athletes with ligaments
presumed to be otherwise healthy, future studies on chronic injuries, specifically in elite
level athletes, are necessary to clarify indications.
A systematic review of complications after UCL reconstruction revealed an overall
complication rate of 10.4%. The most common complication was transient ulnar neuritis
(75.4%), followed by donor site morbidity (12.8%), the need for revision UCL
reconstruction (6.6%), stiffness (2.8%), reactive synovitis (1.4%), hematoma (0.9%), and
ulnar tunnel fracture (0.9%).31 In a 2014 systematic review comparing complications
based on technique, complications occurred in 29.2% of the patients who underwent the
Jobe technique, 19.1% of the patients who underwent the modified Jobe technique, and
6.0% of the patients who underwent the docking technique. Ulnar nerve neuropraxia
was the most common complication, occurring at a rate of 23.6% with the Jobe
technique, 14.4% with the modified Jobe technique, and 2.4% with the docking
technique.38
Mark as Complete
